body:
`amx_on` only checks geometry and CPU support, so every eligible page range executes LDTILECFG/TILERELEASE and packs each query before the dense-page predicate is evaluated. Partial pages, masked/sliding-window pages, and null-mirror fallbacks therefore pay AMX setup plus a 4 KB pack even though every page uses AVX. Could we lazily begin the region and pack Q only when the first page actually satisfies the dense predicate?

— Codex review, submitted at Jeremy’s request

The kernel interface requires each packed-Q buffer to be 64-byte aligned, but `std::vector<uint16_t>` guarantees only `alignof(uint16_t)`. Since each slice is exactly 4096 bytes, every query inherits the base misalignment and TILELOADD can repeatedly straddle cache lines. Could this use a 64-byte-aligned allocator or aligned fixed storage?

— Codex review, submitted at Jeremy’s request

You are right about the structure. `begin_region()` (the call that runs LDTILECFG, the instruction that loads the AMX tile configuration) runs once for every page range with `amx_on` true (self_attention.hpp:1374). Each token's query group is packed at its first visible page, before any page has passed the dense-page test (the test that lets a full 64-token page use the AMX kernel; it lives in `apply_page_tok`, 1564-1566). So a page range with no dense page pays the setup and then does all its work in the AVX fallback loop.

Three details changed after you filed this:
- The gate now also requires the executor to store activations as bf16, not only geometry and CPU support (02208bebcf).
- A pack now writes about 1 KB of live data into the 4 KB buffer. The other 3 KB is padding, zeroed once per thread rather than on every pack (35b3f3caef).
- Pages that are fully masked, or fully outside the sliding window, are skipped before any pack (1394/1397). A missing mirror with `amx_on` true can only happen when the arena's no-throw allocation failed, which is rare. The common fallback cases are partial pages and window-clipped pages, as you said.

We measured the question on the production CPU (Xeon 6962P; results recorded under exec/results/jeremy-measure-20260831 in our campaign repo):
- The LDTILECFG + TILERELEASE pair costs about 229 cycles, roughly 85 ns, paid once per page-range call.
- One pack costs 6.3 ns in the mirror build (it is a 1 KB memcpy); the canonical build's scalar packer costs 63 ns.
- For scale, one dense page's full QK + softmax + PV costs 686 ns (mirror kernel) to 1250 ns (canonical).
- How often the setup is wasted, counted per call during qwen-3-4b decode: 21-24% of AMX-on page-range calls finish with zero AMX pages at 2K and 8K contexts, and 37% in a short run with a 32-token prompt. These are mostly sections holding only the partial tail page, as you predicted.

So the waste is frequent but small. Those calls burn roughly 26-32 microseconds of region setup per decode step, plus at most their share of the pack time, spread across 12 attention worker threads. The upper bound is about 0.5-0.8% of one decode step's CPU time, which is on the order of 0.05% of wall-clock decode. At that size we prefer keeping one uninterrupted tile region per call over threading lazy state through the per-token, per-page hot path, so the code stays as is. If a future model shape shifts the balance (a CPU-served sliding-window model, for example), the first move on record is a ~5-line change: pack only when the page is full, and open the region at the first pack.

Agreed, and fixed in 60d66d9c04. Both packer contracts require a 64-byte-aligned 4 KB buffer (amx_attn_iface.hpp:192 and :253), and this was the only 64-byte contract in that header we did not honor: the `o` and `s` buffers get `alignas(64)` storage (self_attention.hpp:1577, 1655), while the pack buffer was a plain `std::vector<uint16_t>`, which only carries operator new's 16-byte guarantee. We probed it on our glibc: the vector's base landed 48 or 16 bytes past a 64-byte boundary depending on size, never on one. A thread keeps the alignment of its largest resize, so a bad base was permanent for that thread. The slices are 4096 bytes each, so every token inherited the same misalignment, as you said.

The fix is the aligned-storage variant you suggested, in vector form: the element type becomes `struct alignas(64) amx_qpack_slot { uint16_t v[Q_PACK_ELEMS_2048]; }`. C++17 routes over-aligned element types through the aligned operator new, the slot stays exactly 4096 bytes, and the vector's zero-fill on growth preserves the padding-must-stay-zero contract. All five AMX and attention test binaries pass on the production CPU.

Two calibrations, now with the number you would want. First, nothing could crash: the buffer is only read by TILELOADD, which has no architectural alignment requirement, and the packers store with scalar writes and memcpy. Second, we measured the split-row penalty you predicted, with an A/B run of the real qk_mirror kernel at a packed-Q base of +0 vs +16 bytes: the misaligned base costs +9.3 ns per page (+10.6%) when the K page is hot in L1 cache, +3.2 ns per page (+0.5%) with a 512-page K ring resident in L2, and is within noise at RAM residency. Real, small, and gone with the fix.

It may not be measurable today, but will be when we have conditions with TLB pressure, which probably only happens under complex customer scenarios.

+#pragma once

+// src/tron/kernels/amx_attn.cpp, the only translation unit compiled with

+// Note [AMX attention dispatch]
+// ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+// TRON_AMX_DISPATCH adds an opt-in AMX fast path inside apply_page_tok for
+// the dense case only: a full 64-token page, fully visible to the query,
+// inside the sliding window, with geometry head_size == 128 && kv_mul == 4
+// and an executor that stores activations as bf16 (amx_attn::eligible =
+// shape_ok + query_scalar_ok, the one gate shared with the mirror
+// write-through and the mirror-arena allocation).
+// That geometry is the tile identity: one GQA group is 4 q-heads x 128 dims
+// = 512 bf16 = 1024 bytes = exactly one full tile operand, so the guaranteed
+// decode width (one user's GQA group) fills the hardware with zero padding
+// waste. Everything else - incomplete or partially visible pages, pages
+// outside the sliding window, narrow or ineligible geometries - falls
+// through to the existing dotter (AVX-512) loop unchanged. Note the unit is
+// the PAGE, not the query: a query at a low position runs its COMPLETE pages
+// on AMX, while its partial tail page could fall to AVX (the predicate is
+// per (query, page): run_visible_in_software + the dense check in
+// self_attention.hpp).
+//
+// Safety chain, in order:
+//   1. compile-time: TRON_AMX_DISPATCH off -> none of this code is built to
+//      binary.
+//   2. compile-time: the executor's activation scalar. The packers copy Q as
+//      bf16 bit patterns and convert nothing, so executors whose btensor_t
+//      element is float (host) or fp16 (host_fp16) compile no fast path
+//      (query_scalar_ok) and keep the AVX dotter, which reads Q with its own
+//      type.
+//   3. process runtime: available() = CPUID 7.0 EDX bits 22 (AMX-BF16) +
+//      24 (AMX-TILE), XCR0[18:17] (OS tile state), and
+//      arch_prctl(ARCH_REQ_XCOMP_PERM) - a per-PROCESS grant (Linux xstate
+//      rules); result cached. Non-AMX hosts (including AMD: feature bits,
+//      not vendor strings) run the AVX path.
+//   4. kill switch: TRON_AMX_DISABLE=1 forces available() false - used for
body: I will offer my usual complaint when it comes to environment variables: where is this documented other than the source? This sort of thing is incredibly poor in discoverability and ultimately either we should have be better way to expose the configuration surface (e.g. a command-line flag) or document these variables centrally.

@@ -0,0 +1,91 @@
+#pragma once
+// Page-sharing instrumentation: measures how many query tokens of the
+// current minibatch legally attend the SAME physical KV page in one visit -
+// the achievable batching width for the AMX kernels.
+//
+// Compiled in only with -DTRON_PAGE_SHARE_COUNTERS=1. Zero hot-loop cost:
+// callers accumulate plain locals and flush to the global atomics once per
+// apply_page_range call (roughly once per (worker, kv_head, page-range) - a
+// few tens of thousands of flushes per second at most).
+//
+// Dump: automatic at process exit to stderr.
+
+#ifdef TRON_PAGE_SHARE_COUNTERS
+#include <atomic>
+#include <cstdint>
+#include <cstdio>
+
+namespace tron::page_share {
+
+// width histogram buckets for n_visible (query tokens per page visit):
+// [0]=1, [1]=2, [2]=3, [3]=4, [4]=5-8, [5]=9-16, [6]=>16
+inline std::atomic<uint64_t> width_hist[7];
+inline std::atomic<uint64_t> page_visits;     // total (page, kv_head) visits
+inline std::atomic<uint64_t> visible_tokens;  // sum of n_visible = work weight
+inline std::atomic<uint64_t> shared_visits;   // visits with n_visible >= 2
+inline std::atomic<uint64_t> shared_tokens;   // work weight on shared visits
+inline std::atomic<uint64_t> pending_visits;  // visits in the pending phase
body: Why are these global `inline`? What is this supposed to do? I would have thought these would be `extern`.

If I'm not mistaken, this is going to result in a runtime allocation. Usually this is frowned upon but the facts that

1. it's `thread_local`
2. attention workers are a long-lived pool
3. batch sizes are bounded

collectively mean that this allocation will be amortized over many operations, which makes it probably okay.

Still, I do wonder why we don't just handle this consistently with the other intermediates needed by attention and attach it to `attn_accum`. Moreover, we know `max_minibatch_size` statically so surely this should just be an `array`.
Can we not move this out into a distinct helper? This function is already coming up on 200 LoC; let's not make a bad situation even worse.
Why not use `mask_t` here?

The surgery in this function is quite brutal, leading to essentially two distinct control flow paths. This suggests to me that there should be two distinct functions, possibly with commonalities factored out into helpers.

body: Discussed with Ben, will create one document to document all TRON environment variables. The tracking issue is https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/issues/4338

`range_hint` is a cached pointer into a ranged mask. apply_page_tok() uses `range_hint`. The hint makes the lookup of the next range O(1) instead of a binary search, both for the per-page lookup in apply_page_range() and, inside apply_page_tok(), after the walk crosses a range boundary within a page. 

The AMX path never crosses a boundary: is_dense_amx_page() admits a page only when its last token is still below the hinted range's tok_hi, so the whole page sits inside the range which the caller already looked up. 

For such a page the dotter loop would never advance the hint either (it advances only when an entry reaches tok_hi), so the returned hint is unchanged, and it is the same value as the dotter would have returned, and the caller's page_end_hint sequence is identical with AMX on or off. 

Pages with a boundary inside them run on the dotter as before.

I added couple lines of comment to make it clear.
Addressed at https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4265

You are right, sorry for confusion.  The pack is per-worker, per-token scratch for one `apply_page_range` call, which is exactly attn_accum's index space, and nothing in the join or the hardware path depends on it.

It is now a member of attn_accum: `std::vector<amx_qpack_slot> amx_qpack;`, indexed by batch_job_ix like the other arrays.

I kept it a vector rather than a `std::array<amx_qpack_slot, max_minibatch_size>` because the array adds 512 KiB (llama plugin) or 4 MiB (ingested plugins) to every attn_accum instance, i.e. all 55 pool-worker scratchpads per model state plus both copies in every hw_attn_results, for eligible and non-eligible models alike (27.5 MiB or 220 MiB per model state on the 6962P with `--instance 1,2`), while the vector stays at 24 bytes wherever the AMX path never runs.

`uint64_t` bitmap is replaced by `std::bitset<max_minibatch_size> amx_packed` now.

More details: 

- `mask_t` (tron's fixed-width bit set in h/common/mask.hpp) exists only for N in {8, 16, 32, 64, 128} (mask.hpp:252-254, storage table at :31-57), plus `mask_t<512>` and `mask_t<4096>` when TRON_AVX512_ENABLED is defined (mask.hpp:462, :465, :686). 
- `max_minibatch_size` is set per plugin (the per-model compile-time description tron is built against): 128 in llama.hpp:184, 1024 in mock.hpp:98 and in every ingested plugin (a plugin generated by the ingest tool from a model checkpoint; ingest/src/TronCpp.hs:264). 
- self_attention.hpp is compiled once per plugin, so this declaration is compiled with N = 128 and with N = 1024. The declaration sits inside `#ifdef TRON_AMX_DISPATCH` but outside the `if constexpr (amx_eligible)` guard (self_attention.hpp:1300-1341, guard at :1377), so `mask_t<max_minibatch_size>` would not compile for any 1024-token plugin in a build with the option on. 
- The code needs only test and set on a per-call local, and `std::bitset` provides both. Under the libstdc++ layout (8-byte words on x86-64) `std::bitset<128>` is 16 bytes and `std::bitset<1024>` is 128 bytes, the same storage as the old `uint64_t` array. The comment at self_attention.hpp:1328-1331 records this reason.

body: Yes, this is fixed now,  AMX buffer type is tron::bf16 instead of uint16_t.

As discussed in the walkthrough yesterday, `apply_page_tok` keeps the shared prologue and dispatches dense pages to `apply_dense_amx_page`, the dotter loop (the existing AVX-512 per-token loop) stays inline and unchanged. 

We compared the two side by side, noted that the per-head softmax and commit loops differ between the paths (the AMX path folds the PV kernel's output where the dotter folds `scaled_v` inside the same loop), and were OK with the current split. Resolving on that basis.

body:
I will keep this in mind when working on AMX improvement. 

BTW this document is being removed, Ben asked me to create another document which lists all TRON environment variables, tracked at https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/issues/4338
While technically this could rather be a statically-sized `std::array` I suppose `vector` is defensible given that we may not use this storage at all. A single allocation seems like a fine trade-off.

As of array vs vector:
- vector costs 24 bytes in every scratchpad that never runs the AMX path
- array costs 512 KiB (llama plugin) or 4 MiB (ingested plugins) in each of the 55 scratchpads

Discussed briefly with Ben at standup, this comment is resolved.
